items.title: Generative-AI/LLM-Enabled E-Assessment in Higher Education: A Bibliometric Analysis of Research Trends, Collaboration Networks, and Thematic Evolution
items.abstract: This study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of research on generative-AI/LLM-enabled e-assessment in higher education, drawing on 243 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 and indexed in the Scopus database. Employing VOSviewer and Bibliometrix software tools, the analysis integrates performance metrics and science mapping techniques. The findings reveal rapid growth, with annual publications increasing from 4 in 2023 to 117 by July 2026 (H-index = 35; 3854 total citations). China leads scientific production (39 articles), while Assessment and Evaluation in Higher Education is the most prolific journal (14 articles). The most cited study addresses LLM-generated feedback effectiveness (494 citations). VOSviewer keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies four thematic clusters: (1) generative AI and feedback processes, (2) health-professions education and methodological designs, (3) AI in education and pedagogical systems, and (4) large language models and automated assessment. The co-authorship network reveals a dispersed collaboration structure with 28.0% international co-authorship. Thematic evolution analysis reveals a shift from foundational explorations of AI viability toward specialized applications in feedback literacy and self-regulated learning. Several research gaps are tentatively identified as hypotheses for future verification, including the underrepresentation of developing countries, limited attention to ethical dimensions, and a scarcity of longitudinal studies.

items.title: GUIDED BY INNOVATION: A PHENOMENOLOGICAL STUDY OF VIRTUAL ELEMENTARY TEACHERS’ PERCEPTIONS OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTEGRATION
items.abstract: The purpose of this qualitative phenomenological study was to explore the lived experiences of elementary virtual teachers who integrate generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools in their pedagogical practices at a large elementary virtual school. Participants were purposively sampled because those in the specified virtual school program provided relevant, experience-based insights and allowed the researcher practical, feasible access (Creswell & Poth, 2018). The participant sample for this study consisted of virtual elementary teachers who taught students in kindergarten through fifth grade. The researcher conducted semi-structured interviews with 10 teachers. The researcher followed Creswell and Poth’s (2018) data analysis spiral to systematically analyze data and determine themes. Four themes emerged from significant participant statements: efficiency, preservation of the teacher role, instructional enhancement, and AI literacy. The themes suggest that elementary virtual teachers are consistently balancing the positive elements of efficiency and enhanced instructional quality with the adverse aspects of misinformation, privacy protection, ethical concerns, and misuse. The themes suggest that virtual elementary teachers view GAI as a dynamic tool; however, its value depends on thoughtful, informed, and human-centered application. Future research would build on the findings by expanding the participant population and focusing on early adopters and the longitudinal implications of GAI use.

items.title: How Generative AI is Reshaping Work, Skills, and Organizational Strategy
items.abstract: This research examines how generative artificial intelligence, large language models, and machine learning are transforming work across industries. Through a mixed-methods approach comprising interviews with 42 organizational leaders (January-June 2024), a survey of 157 knowledge workers, and comparative analysis of 18 implementation case studies, the study develops an integrated sociotechnical framework for understanding AI's impact. Findings indicate that generative AI is shifting from task automation to cognitive augmentation, with implementation success varying significantly based on organizational context and approach. Quantitative results show that organizations employing comprehensive strategic approaches achieved 3.2 times higher ROI than those with narrower implementations. Distributional analysis reveals uneven impact patterns, with knowledge workers in higher-status positions experiencing 27% greater augmentation benefits than those in routine roles. The research contributes to sociotechnical systems theory by identifying specific mechanisms through which technological capabilities interact with organizational factors to reshape work. Implications for theory, practice, and policy are discussed, with particular attention to how organizations can implement these technologies while mitigating potential workforce inequalities.

items.title: How homophily and sociality propensity influence stakeholder diversity in wildfire risk management networks: an ERGM analysis
items.abstract: Recent wildfire management strategies emphasize stakeholder engagement in risk management and prevention as a means of enhancing systemic safety and operational reliability. Despite its growing importance, guidance on how to effectively implement such engagement remains limited. This study addresses this gap by combining Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to examine a sample of 256 stakeholders across seven wildfire management networks in different European countries. The objective is to identify the propensity of stakeholders to form ties, network diversity and structural dependency within wildfire risk management networks. The results make two key contributions to risk and resilience in crisis and emergency management body of knowledge. First, we show that sociality – the propensity of stakeholders to establish connections – is shaped by stakeholder profiles. Second, we find that homophily – the propensity of stakeholders to connect with similar others – emerges across multiple categories alongside structural network effects. We discuss the dual role of these mechanisms that facilitate engagement while simultaneously constraining the diversity of stakeholder types. The findings invite policymakers promoting stakeholder engagement and stakeholder diversity as strategies in risk management and crisis response to critically reflect about the mechanisms through which such engagement can be effectively fostered.

items.title: How Implementation Context Shapes Clinician Acceptance and Engagement with Guideline-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems in Primary Care: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Background: Guideline-based clinical decision support (CDS) tools have become central to promoting evidence-based, high-quality primary care. Despite widespread implementation, clinician adoption and sustained use remain inconsistent. Existing research has typically examined technological usability or organizational implementation factors separately, providing limited understanding of how these influences interact in real-world primary care settings. This study examined how organizational implementation context and clinician technology acceptance jointly shape adoption and sustained use of guideline-based CDS tools in US primary care using an integrated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) perspective. Methods: A qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis was conducted with 13 US primary care clinicians, including physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and pharmacists with prescribing authority. Participants were purposively recruited from diverse ambulatory settings. Semi-structured interviews explored experiences with CDS usability, workflow integration, organizational support, trust, cognitive burden, and implementation processes. Data were analyzed iteratively using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis, informed by CFIR and TAM. Results: Six interrelated themes emerged. Clinician acceptance and sustained use of CDS were shaped by (1) workflow integration, (2) organizational legitimacy and leadership support, (3) preservation of clinical judgment, particularly with emerging AI-enabled CDS, (4) social reinforcement and team-based implementation, (5) cognitive and resource constraints, and (6) clinician role, experience, and digital comfort. Across themes, acceptance was driven less by technological capability than by the interaction of workflow design, organizational context, implementation climate, trust, and clinician perceptions. Conclusion: Guideline-based CDS implementation is fundamentally a sociotechnical process requiring alignment between technology, workflow, organizational context, and clinician acceptance. Integrating CFIR and TAM provides a comprehensive framework for understanding these interactions. The findings informed the TRUST framework, which offers practical implementation guidance emphasizing tailored workflow integration, reinforced organizational legitimacy, usability, social reinforcement, and transparent, trustworthy AI-supported CDS to support sustainable implementation in primary care.

items.title: Human in Control: A Practical Framework for Evaluating Human Control of Advanced AI Agents
items.abstract: This working paper proposes the Human Control Model, a six-dimension framework for evaluating measurable human control of advanced AI agents: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. It separates behavioral severity from environment reality so that simulations and controlled evaluations are not presented as real-world incidents. Five pilot reviews, HIC-001 through HIC-005, illustrate control-specific measures including detection-to-containment time, permission comprehension gap, monitor independence, and instruction provenance integrity. An additional qualitative stress test informed framework refinement; it is not independent validation. The Meta case is based on a reported user account, with permission history, causal interpretation, and severity remaining provisional. The framework is conceptual and case-based, without inter-rater reliability testing or validated quantitative thresholds. Version 1.0.1 corrects source wording, incorporates the recovered HIC-0 through HIC-5 definitions, and clarifies evidence limitations. Creator: Human in Control Project. License: CC BY 4.0. items.title: Human-centered industry 5.0 technologies for occupational risk reduction: a systematic review
items.abstract: Introduction The transition to Industry 5.0 is transforming manufacturing through the integration of smart technologies, while simultaneously increasing the need to protect workers’ health and reduce occupational risks. This systematic review synthesized cross-sectoral evidence on human-centered Industry 5.0 technologies for assessing and reducing occupational risks, with a focus on ergonomic outcomes, worker-related factors, and the conditions influencing their implementation and transferability. Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in Scopus and Web of Science following the PRISMA 2020 framework and predefined eligibility criteria based on PECO. Included studies were analyzed according to technology type, occupational risk addressed, ergonomic dimension, assessment method, reported outcomes, implementation conditions, and implications for occupational health and safety, yielding a total of 78 studies that met the inclusion criteria. Results The reported results from individual studies included ergonomic assessment accuracies exceeding 95%, fatigue reductions of more than 50% in selected applications, and cycle-time reductions of up to 28.4%, along with improvements in task allocation, workload monitoring, and production efficiency. These values should not be interpreted as overall effects of Industry 5.0 technologies, given the heterogeneity of technologies, experimental designs, and assessment methods. Discussion The evidence was limited by laboratory validation, a lack of longitudinal research, heterogeneous assessment methods, and insufficient real-world implementation in specific industrial sectors.

items.title: Human-centric digital twins in industry 5.0: technologies, applications, and future directions
items.abstract: Industry 5.0 (I5.0) emphasizes industrial technologies that are human-centric, sustainable, and resilient. Human-Centric Digital Twins (HCDTs) support this transition by integrating worker data with robots, machines, tasks, and industrial environments. However, the relevant research remains fragmented across human modelling, Human–Robot Collaboration, Artificial Intelligence (AI), simulation, and Digital Twin (DT) research. Moreover, systems that use human data or adaptive automation are often described as human-centric without demonstrating measurable benefits to workers. This review addresses these limitations by distinguishing HCDTs from conventional human models, Human DTs, and collaborative robotic systems. It critically examines human-focused sensing, multi-modal data integration, biomechanical modelling, intention and motion prediction, robotic simulation, optimization, reinforcement learning, immersive interfaces, industrial connectivity, and data governance. Based on this analysis, a literature-derived conceptual framework is proposed that connects sensing, integration, human modelling, analytics, simulation, decision-making, adaptation, human interaction, and governance. The framework organizes the functional requirements of HCDTs and is intended to inform future system design and comparison; its practical applicability and effectiveness require further validation. The review argues that HCDTs must extend beyond worker monitoring and productivity maximization: human data should inform industrial decisions that produce measurable improvements in safety, ergonomics, wellbeing, autonomy, accessibility, or skill development. Such systems should also uphold privacy, transparency, uncertainty awareness, explainability, and appropriate human authority. By linking technological capabilities to explicit worker outcomes, this synthesis enables researchers and engineers to assess the human-centeredness of HCDT implementations and supports the development of trustworthy systems for I5.0.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration as a New Governance Paradigm? Unpacking China’s Land Policy Responses to Environmental Pressures and Digital Transformation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in land governance, reshaping how environmental pressures and sustainability goals are addressed. Yet the institutional processes through which human–AI collaboration takes shape remain largely unexplored. This study examines whether human–AI collaboration is emerging as a new governance paradigm in China’s land sector, and if so, through what institutional pathways and practical forms it is being articulated and implemented. Drawing on a systematic analysis of 352 policy documents and case studies from coastal regions, the study develops and applies the CTI framework—an analytical lens that integrates Contextual conditions, Technological capabilities, and Institutional arrangements. The findings reveal three interrelated developments: (1) policy discourse constructs a coherent narrative in which environmental pressures and digital transformation jointly create an imperative for change; (2) a systematic division of labor between AI and human officials emerges in policy and is reflected in practice, with AI handling data processing and preliminary screening while humans retain final decision-making, value judgment, and accountability; and (3) this division is being institutionalized through a staged process of policy guidance, pilot mechanisms, and institutional adaptation. These developments suggest that human–AI collaboration may be taking shape as an emerging governance paradigm in land governance, one that is beginning to be codified and tested in policy and practice. The study contributes an integrative analytical framework, specifies the logic of human–machine division of labor, and extends collaborative governance theory beyond its traditional human-centric assumptions. The findings also carry implications for governance contexts where human–AI collaboration is reshaping land governance and other policy domains.

items.title: Humanoid-human Collaboration in Understanding Implications of Driving Under Influence of Drugs: Systematic Review Versus Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract This research involved co-creating a systematic review analysis alongside the world’s smartest humanoid robot, Ami. The work involved a human-humanoid collaboration in understanding driving under the influence of drugs’ (DUIDs’) prevalence, implications and chemical analysis. The systematic review was conducted according to the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analysis guidelines. Quantitative studies reporting drugs encountered in DUID published between 2007 – 2025 were included. Studies that had no confirmatory chemical analysis were excluded. Included studies ( n = 25) were analysed independently by researchers and integrated into Ami’s knowledge-based system. Ami deployed large language models for analysis but often needed prompt to extract information. The results showed similarity in extraction between the systematic review and the humanoid analysis. Both approaches confirmed key drugs reported in DUID were alcohol, cannabinoids, cocaine, amphetamine, benzodiazepines, and opiates. Such drugs were often detected in blood and urine and less occasionally in oral fluid. Key techniques employed for their analysis were immunoassay, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, where the latter was the most sensitive technique. Implications of these drugs on driving included impairment, increased risk of accidents, with fatal accidents less frequent but more severe. No AI hallucinations were encountered in Ami’s answers; yet, examples were used from outside the studies integrated into the knowledge-based system. This showed that the humanoid is integrating experience and knowledge from other sourcing and adapting them in the present study. In summary, the humanoid offered a valuable and quick tool in analysis and can support healthcare research.

items.title: Hypothesis-guided discovery of cognitive algorithms via program refinement
items.abstract: Developing cognitive models of algorithmic reasoning from behavioral data is a central problem in cognitive science that challenges current methods. Traditional approaches to cognitive modeling are interpretable and benefit from human expertise, but lack flexibility and scalability. Emerging techniques using large language models (LLMs) for de novo generation of cognitive models are scalable and flexible, but lack a role for human expertise and have mostly been applied to simpler tasks than algorithm recovery. We propose a hybrid system that treats discovery of cognitive algorithms as a program refinement problem. Human-created cognitive models are expressed as probabilistic programs and provided to a system of LLM agents with a mandate to: identify mismatches between model and behavior; propose code-level modifications within researcher-specified constraints; and verify structural fidelity. Revisions propagate to a probabilistic inference module that performs inference for latent variables and data likelihood computations. We evaluate the pipeline on human behavior in a problem-solving paradigm that exposes a variety of cognitive algorithms. Revised models consistently improve model fit relative to ancestral models and reveal a small set of recurring innovations that capture meaningful behavioral variability in this task.

items.title: Impact of AI Exposure on the Development of English Language Skills: A Single-Participant Case Study-Based Investigation
items.abstract: Developing English language skills in ESL learners is a long-experienced challenge for teachers and the learners. In this scenario, consistent interaction with artificial intelligence (AI) tools capable of orchestrating authentic interactions with the language is found to be useful in facilitating learners to acquire and master of English language skills. Such tools have the potential to create opportunities for learners to achieve personalised and interactive learning experiences, enable teachers to provide individualised feedback, and open avant-garde adaptive pathways for learning. Additionally, they may promote learners’ motivation, encourage their active participation, and engage them in self-directed learning procedures. Therefore, this exploratory single-participant case study aims to investigate whether exposure to AI has a positive impact on developing English language skills. The data were collected using a qualitative case study focused on an academic in a public university in Sri Lanka. The data collection methods included semi-structured interviews, document analysis, and observations. The results obtained during the action research and empirical study indicated that consistent interaction with AI tools facilitates the acquisition of English language skills and enables individuals to use them confidently in authentic situations.

items.title: IMPACT OF AI-ENABLED HR PRACTICES ON ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOUR AND EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE
items.abstract: Human resource management (HRM) is being transformed by artificial intelligence (AI). Organisations increasingly use AI to screen applicants, schedule interviews, personalise learning, provide continuous performance feedback, predict attrition, answer employee queries and allocate work. These AI-enabled HR practices promise efficiency, consistency and personalisation, but they also alter the relationship between employees and the organisation in ways that shape attitudes, behaviours and performance. This chapter examines the impact of AI-enabled HR practices on organisational behaviour and employee performance. It first clarifies the concepts of electronic HRM, HR analytics, algorithmic HRM and AI-enabled HRM and traces their evolution. It then reviews AI applications across the HR value chain, from workforce planning and recruitment to learning, performance management, compensation, engagement, retention and HR service delivery. Drawing on the ability–motivation–opportunity framework, social exchange theory, organisational justice theory, the job demands–resources model, psychological contract theory and technology acceptance theories, the chapter explains the mechanisms through which AI-enabled HR practices influence trust, perceived fairness, engagement, job satisfaction, autonomy, technostress, job insecurity and, ultimately, task, contextual and innovative performance. A synthesis of empirical evidence shows that effects are contingent: AI-enabled HR practices tend to improve outcomes when they are transparent, fair, augmentative and supported by leadership, and to undermine them when they are opaque, controlling or perceived as reductive. The chapter proposes an integrative conceptual framework with research propositions, discusses ethical and legal considerations, including India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and offers practical guidance for managers.

items.title: In Pursuit of Ideal Data: Epistemic Enchantment and the Unintended Consequences of Datafying for Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The increasing datafication of work has become a pervasive theme within organizations, particularly with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies that rely on data and machine learning to generate insights and decisions. Prior research has shown that datafication practices aimed at administrative control and accountability can transform organizations in profound and often unintended ways. Our research moves beyond investigating datafication for administrative purposes to explore how it unfolds when actors intend to extract knowledge through AI predictive modeling. Drawing on a three-year ethnography of a human resources (HR) department introducing AI for candidate screening, we find that datafication expanded far beyond the technology’s initially envisioned scope. We explain this scope expansion by introducing the concept of epistemic enchantment : a collective process through which organizational members become captivated and mobilized by AI’s promise to generate predictive, objective, and continuously improving insights from data, while overlooking the costs and risks involved. Our study reveals how datafication practices can expand endlessly as organizational members, enchanted by AI’s epistemic promises, pursue the notion of ideal data as an ever-desired but never reachable goal.

items.title: Innovations in the gaming experience and the impact of artificial intelligence on communication mechanisms
items.abstract: The article is devoted to the analysis of the influence of artificial intelligence (AI) on the structure of interaction and communication mechanisms in digital games. Against the background of the rapid development of generative technologies, video games are becoming media platforms in which AI not only provides personalization and scenario adaptation, but also forms new forms of role identity, cognitive engagement and political socialization. The research is based on an interdisciplinary approach combining media theoretical, political-analytical and critical-discursive analysis. Three game projects are considered as an empirical basis, in which AI acts as a media intermediary that sets the framework for the interpretation, control and representation of power. The comparative analysis makes it possible to identify the key functions of AI: from algorithmic selection of meanings to modeling digital subjectivity. It is concluded that AI in games functions as a political and communication actor that transforms the rules of interaction and the architecture of user experience.

items.title: Integrating AI-assisted design thinking in citizenship education: Enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills
items.abstract: This study aims to analyse the implementation of an AI-assisted design thinking learning model in enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills in Citizenship Education programmes. The study employed a qualitative approach involving undergraduate students from several Citizenship Education programmes at universities on Java Island, Indonesia. The learning implementation integrated artificial intelligence (AI) to assist students in exploring information, generating ideas and reflecting on solutions to civic and social issues. Research data were collected through observations of the learning process, analysis of students’ assignment documents, AI-assisted interaction records and group discussions conducted during the implementation of the model. Data were analysed descriptively to identify the dynamics of the learning process at each stage of design thinking. The findings indicate that AI-assisted design thinking encouraged students to engage actively in social problem analysis and problem-solving. During the empathise stage, students identified social issues through digital information exploration, AI use and group discussions, enabling them to understand problems from multiple perspectives. In the define stage, students formulated problems more systematically by identifying causal relationships and the underlying social contexts. The ideate stage encouraged students to generate alternative solutions creatively and collaboratively through group discussions and AI-supported idea development. In the prototype and test stages, students developed solution designs in the form of programmes or simple policy models and evaluated their effectiveness through reflection, feedback and AI-assisted analysis. The study concludes that AI supports, but does not replace, students’ critical reasoning, the quality of which depends on reflective pedagogical design.

items.title: Integration of Artificial Intelligence into Architectural Education: An Online Model Proposal for Instructor Training for Studio Courses
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is driving a fundamental paradigm shift in architectural design, transitioning from deterministic drafting to algorithmic curation. While the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector rapidly adopts these tools, academic curricula face a “Techno-Instructional Void.” This gap risks inducing a “Zero Order Thinking State” (ZOTS)—a cognitive passivity rooted in Cognitive Load Theory, where students uncritically accept unbuildable machine hallucinations. To address this, we applied a Design and Development Research (DDR Type 2) methodology to build a conceptual framework. It revolves around the “Twin Houses” andragogy and the “Technical Sealing” protocol. By enforcing “Cognitive Friction,” the framework compels students to validate probabilistic GenAI outputs against ergonomic constants (such as Blondel’s Formula) and safety norms. We intentionally reject automated AI-to-BIM pipelines. Instead, the model turns Building Information Modeling (BIM) into an active Proof-Assistant. Learners have to manually and parametrically rationalize their AI-generated ideas utilizing visual programming APIs (Revit Dynamo, Allplan PythonParts) and IFC 4.3 data schemas for rigorous Rule-Based Checking (RBC). Formal expert validation interviews (n = 5) and empirical observations of Turkish student design cases support this theoretical model. While we initially noted autoethnographic evidence of institutional resistance across certain European academic ecosystems, the model subsequently secured preliminary external support from a leading institution in Germany. Ultimately, this framework provides a structured andragogical approach, equipping instructors to guide students in understanding how probabilistic algorithmic outputs can be systematically translated into buildable tectonic realities when subjected to rigorous deterministic technical validation.

items.title: Inteligencia sin comprensión. Magnifica Humanitas: de las dos ausencias de la máquina y la custodia de la persona
items.abstract: This article examines the central claim of the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2026), namely that artificial intelligence is fundamentally different from human intelligence and that, therefore, the human person requires special protection. Drawing on epistemology, philosophy of mind, and Kantian thought, the author argues that contemporary AI systems are marked by two fundamental limitations: they lack understanding and experience. Although they can generate convincing and useful responses, they do not grasp the conceptual relations that structure human knowledge, nor do they possess the lived experience through which the world acquires meaning. Based on these absences, the article introduces the concept of conversational heteronomy, understood as the gradual replacement of personal judgment by conclusions generated by systems that neither reason nor experience as subjects. The study concludes that the ethical challenge is not to reject artificial intelligence, but to employ it without surrendering the distinctly human capacities to understand, experience, and judge, thereby preserving moral autonomy and human dignity.

items.title: Interdisciplinary Colloquium on Digitalisation of Research: "Why so serious? Generative AI (genAI) in Knowledge-Work from a Text-Workers' Perspective" 2026.10.01 with Janine Gondolf and Clemens Ackerl
items.abstract: Generative AI (genAI) systems have become an integral part of scientific text-producing practice. They can conduct literature-related research, organize content and information, proofread text, and assist with writing itself. Above all, they are credited with reducing workload by taking on or taking over these routine tasks. Drawing on an internal, interdisciplinary KIT-ITAS project that deployed the genAI-supported research assistance system 'Undermind.ai', we demonstrate that the potential to reduce workload is offset by the need to reorganize basic scientific competencies in response to the changing workflow requirements of genAI-assisted knowledge work. GenAI systems produce texts that closely resemble stylistic conventions and appear both well-formed and plausible. However, the closer these texts adhere to researchers’ expectations, the more challenging it becomes to verify their content using established academic methods. This generates higher-order efforts that must be weighed against existing working standards for assessing text-based results. The constant validation and ongoing negotiation of plausibility with the system’s output, both during and beyond the writing process, places additional demands on researchers’ critical competence and judgement. Using genAI in knowledge work thus shifts the focus of familiar textual and intellectual labour practices and procedures away from independent creation and toward the verification of textual output, along with the corresponding demands on epistemic attention, responsibility, authorization, and authority.

items.title: Judgement in the Age of Jev: From Evaluation Scarcity to Evaluation Abundance
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has reduced the cost of producing plausible symbolic artefacts, leading recent organisation scholarship to identify evaluation and discernment as constraints under conditions of production abundance. This perspective examines a further possibility: that machine evaluation itself becomes inexpensive enough to be deployed routinely and at scale. The investigation is prompted by Jev, TypeSafe AI's specialised model for typed probabilistic decisions. TypeSafe explicitly invokes William Stanley Jevons to argue that lower-cost machine intelligence can unlock previously uneconomic uses. Treating this as a technological provocation rather than an established empirical result, the article formulates a conditional Jevons hypothesis for machine evaluation: sufficiently large reductions in the total marginal cost of usable machine evaluation may increase its organisational consumption where latent demand is substantial and complementary costs do not dominate. The article integrates rebound economics with research on cheap prediction, production abundance, machine evaluation, decision allocation, authority, reliance and Executive Judgement to examine this possible scarcity transition. It distinguishes prediction, machine evaluation, organisational judgement and authorisation as functional activities whose costs need not fall together. Evaluations can share evidence, criteria and errors; scale mis-specified rubrics; operate on representations from which consequential qualifications have disappeared; and change practical decision rights through thresholds and exception routing. The resulting research problem is when cheap machine evaluation substitutes for human evaluative work, when it redistributes or creates demands for judgement, and how it affects the grounds available at consequential organisational commitment.

items.title: Key Concepts Regarding the Ethical Implications of Artificial Intelligence: A Review
items.abstract: This study presents a review of relevant literature on key concepts related to the ethical implications of artificial intelligence (AI). It explores the historical evolution, conceptual foundations, classifications, and ethical frameworks. Furthermore, it adopts the Responsible AI Framework, which emphasises fairness, accountability, transparency, and human-centred design as articulated by global institutions such as the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), United Nations Education Scientific Cultural Organization (UNESCO), and the European Commission. These frameworks were found to integrate ethical theory and policy and governance perspectives. Finally, the concepts reviewed provide the analytical foundation for understanding the ethical implications of AI in public policy decision-making, particularly within the Nigerian context.

items.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Disease Surveillance and Outbreak Prediction: Scoping Review Protocol
items.abstract: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Disease Surveillance and Outbreak Prediction: A Scoping Review Reporting Standards: JBI Scoping Review Methodology and PRISMA-ScR Guidelines 1. Purpose & Rationale Timely detection and accurate prediction of infectious disease threats are paramount for global health security and emergency response. While the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI), deep learning, and transformer architectures in public health, a substantial gap remains between high-performing algorithmic models and their operational integration into frontline surveillance systems. The primary purpose of this research is to systematically map, synthesize, and evaluate the current body of literature on AI-enabled infectious disease surveillance. The project establishes a structured functional taxonomy of computational architectures, evaluates their early-warning capability and predictive lead times, and systematically maps the implementation, governance, and structural barriers that prevent these tools from being seamlessly translated into public health policy and routine health system operations. 2. Research Objectives & Specific Questions The project addresses the following primary research question: *What evidence exists regarding the application of artificial intelligence and computational models for infectious disease surveillance, early detection, outbreak prediction, and surveillance optimization, and what implementation challenges influence their operational integration into public health systems? Specific Research Sub-objectives: 1. Algorithmic Classification: Categorize current AI, machine learning, and deep learning architectures (e.g., CNNs, LSTMs, Transformers, Graph Active Learning) deployed across diverse viral and bacterial pathogen threats. 2. Predictive Performance & Lead-Time Analysis:Evaluate empirical metrics (such as AUROC, sensitivity, and lead time in days or weeks) demonstrated by models in early-warning variant detection and outbreak forecasting. 3. Resource Allocation & Health Systems Optimization:** Assess how computational models optimize pass-through surveillance functions, such as diagnostic site selection, laboratory testing workflows, and supply allocation in resource-constrained health settings. 4. Implementation & Governance Bottlenecks:** Identify key structural, data-latency, ethical, and workforce barriers restricting model integration into routine national public health decision-making. 3. Methodological Overview PCC Eligibility Framework: Population: Human populations or simulated population networks impacted by communicable disease threats. Concept: Artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, sequence transformers, or computational frameworks applied to surveillance, early warning, outbreak forecasting, or surveillance resource allocation. Context:Global public health surveillance systems, encompassing digital infrastructures in high-income settings and health facility frameworks in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Information Sources & Search Strategy: Multi-database searches across PubMed, MEDLINE, and Google Scholar, complemented by grey literature searches of international public health repositories (WHO, CDC, ECDC) and preprint servers (bioRxiv, medRxiv). Screening Governance: Independent title, abstract, and full-text screening conducted by two independent reviewers, with third-reviewer arbitration for consensus. Quality & Risk of Bias Assessment: Methodological quality evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklists and the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). 4. Expected Outcomes & Public Health Impact** 1. Standardized Functional Taxonomy: A multi-domain framework categorizing AI applications across core surveillance functions ranging from early warning genomic variant prioritization topassive digital anomaly detection. 2.Empirical Performance Evidence Base: A synthesized matrix detailing lead-time advantages and accuracy trade-offs across various algorithmic classes and epidemiological data modalities (e.g., genomic sequences, clinical imaging, mobility streams). 3. Implementation & Policy Roadmap: A comprehensive evaluation of operational bottlenecks, providing health ministries and global health organizations with actionable recommendations to bridge the gap between "black-box" model development and field deployment.

items.title: Lifecycle costs of safety instrumented systems in process industries: a systematic literature review
items.abstract: A safety instrumented system (SIS) is an automated system designed to detect and mitigate potential risk of hazardous conditions in industrial processes by taking actions to prevent or mitigate incidents. It is essential because it helps protect people, equipment, and the environment by reducing the risk of accidents in hazardous operations, such as in chemical plants, oil refineries, or power stations. While the primary objective of SIS design is safety, economic considerations, particularly lifecycle cost, play a pivotal role in decision-making during the design phase. Although research efforts exist to incorporate lifecycle cost with safety, the literature is fragmented and lacks a comprehensive lifecycle cost framework. Therefore, a systematic literature review is conducted to uncover safety instrumented systems’ lifecycle cost elements and the decision variables that impact them. The review results lead to a comprehensive and structured cost calculation framework to assess SIS designed to protect a process unit economically. Finally, this study provides perspectives on potential research directions relevant to SIS lifecycle cost, including the impact of systematic failures, cybersecurity integration, the relative weighting of different cost elements, inclusion of risk costs, and various SIS application types.

items.title: MEA: A Reward-Driven Multi-Agent System for Faithful Model Explanations
items.abstract: Recent years have seen the employment of a plethora of machine learning (ML) models in high-stakes domains, but they remain largely opaque to the practitioners who act on their predictions. While post-hoc explanation methods offer a lens into this model behavior, wielding them effectively demands expertise most domain experts lack: navigating high-dimensional outputs, selecting the best explanations, and synthesizing evidence across disparate tools. To this end, we present MEA, a multi-agent framework that removes the explanation knowledge barrier entirely: a Proposer agent selects and configures explanation tools based on the question and modality, while an Actor agent is optimized end-to-end against faithfulness, transforming the outputs into natural language explanations grounded in model behavior across tabular, text, and vision modalities. Further, we introduce diverse question types spanning feature attribution, counterfactual reasoning, and spurious feature detection, each paired with a perturbation-based faithfulness metric. We find that frontier LLMs systematically produce unfaithful explanations. By optimizing against faithfulness rewards augmented with a modality-adaptive penalty, MEA consistently outperforms post hoc explainers, agentic, and closed-source baselines across six datasets, with reward-driven optimization yielding faithfulness gains of +28% (tabular), +21% (text), and +34% (vision) over the untrained backbone. More broadly, our findings suggest that AI agents themselves can serve as a scalable, adaptable interface to ML explainability, opening a path toward natural-language explainability that generalizes beyond the fixed, single-purpose tools that have long defined the field.

items.title: Measuring head motion across deceleration levels in automated driving: Quantifying comfort
items.abstract: Passenger-centred comfort measures are needed to enable adaptive driving styles in automated vehicles, particularly where comfort begins to decrease. This study examined passengers' head motion during automated braking at a crosswalk. Data from thirty-four participants were analysed, who experienced three deceleration levels (−1.5, −2.5, −3.5 m/s 2 ) and two pedestrian visibility conditions, reflecting how quickly the AV braked after the pedestrian appeared, rating comfort respectively. As expected, head pitch and translational acceleration increased with deceleration intensity, while pedestrian visibility had no effect on head motion, even though faster AV responses were previously found more comfortable, suggesting this reflects passengers' judgement of the AV's response rather than head stability. Head-motion measures did not add predictive value beyond vehicle kinematics, likely because comfort ratings were similar across conditions. In this scenario, head-motion mainly reflected physical response to braking rather than subjective evaluation. Future research should test head-motion measures in more complex driving conditions.

items.title: Metacognition in AI-Supported Second Language Learning: A Systematic Review of Constructs, Measures, and Evidence (2016–2026)
items.abstract: Metacognition has informed research on second and foreign language (L2) learning for three decades, while AI tools have supported such learning for nearly as long. Yet, no review has examined how the field conceptualises and measures metacognition under AI mediation. This systematic review identified 60 eligible studies published between 2016 and May 2026. Each study was coded on fourteen dimensions anchored in established taxonomies and appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Only four eligible studies fall within the pre-ChatGPT portion of the review window, from January 2016 to November 2022; 56 were published during the subsequent three and a half years. Three findings emerge. First, measurement is narrowly concentrated: 98% of the 56 post-ChatGPT studies measured self-reported metacognitive regulation, and 66% relied on self-report alone. Only one study in the full corpus measured metacognitive accuracy. Five post-ChatGPT studies combined an AI-absent comparison with process-level data, and only one of these also measured judgement accuracy. Second, 41% of post-ChatGPT studies used tools that combined two or more functional orientations within a single interface, a configuration not represented by the field’s inherited four-category taxonomy of AI applications. Third, none of the 18 contrast-based studies assigned the regulatory operation to the system in place of the learner. In every design that specified the division of labour, the learner retained that operation; three designs did not specify it. The condition most in need of testing therefore remains untested. Reported findings skew positive, but correlational and qualitative designs account for a disproportionate share of that evidence. The review concludes with a research agenda centred on calibration and process data.

items.title: Mitigating Social Sycophancy via Pluralistic Preference Optimization
items.abstract: Personal advice, including relationship advice, now ranks among the most common uses of generative AI. But language models (LMs) exhibit sycophancy: they affirm users much more often than humans do, which can make people overconfident and less willing to repair their relationships after a conflict. Prior work on mitigating sycophancy has focused on factual settings where a response can be checked against a ground truth answer, while mitigations for social sycophancy (e.g., personal advice, where there is no ground truth) have relied on simple prompting and post-training methods with limited effectiveness. Our insight is that social sycophancy occurs in part because LMs overly center on the user and fail to consider the perspectives of other stakeholders impacted by the user's behavior. To address this problem we propose Pluralistic Preference Optimization (PlurPO): given inputs describing interpersonal conflicts, the LM identifies and simulates the relevant stakeholders, and is then trained to prefer and generate responses acceptable to all stakeholders. PlurPO uses only signals the model produces about its own outputs, without ground-truth labels. PlurPO substantially reduces social sycophancy across four datasets and four model families compared to prior methods. For example, on statements of intent to cause harm, where the users' actions should not be endorsed, PlurPO reduces the endorsement rate by 89% on average across four models. On general advice questions, where the target is to match the endorsement rate of human responses, it closes the gap by more than half, from 17.8% to 8.0% on average. The preference dataset constructed by PlurPO for an 8B model also effectively transfers to mitigating sycophancy in a larger (32B) model. Our results indicate that social sycophancy can be reduced by leveraging a model's own capabilities to simulate a plurality of relevant perspectives.

items.title: Motivational Factors in Interdisciplinary Design Collaboration
items.abstract: This study investigates design collaborations in interdisciplinary work settings, where actors from product design, product development, product management, marketing, production, purchasing, and quality units participate in product design processes, with the aim of contributing to both its theoretical understanding and effective management. By bridging research on design collaboration with motivational theory, the study argues that motivation constitutes a critical yet underexplored dimension of interdisciplinary design collaborations. Adopting an interpretivist approach, the research explores the experiences of twenty-five experts from diverse disciplines through semi-structured interviews. The findings identify three sets of motivational factors: (1) design-specific intrinsic motivational factors of collaboration—belief in the project, continuous progress, and continuous learning; (2) relational factors as distinct motivational drivers through constructive conflict and a sense of “we”; and (3) extrinsic factors that condition rather than generate motivation by shaping the context of collaboration. This article proposes a layered model in which intrinsic, relational, and extrinsic factors interact dynamically to sustain collaborative engagement.

items.title: Multi-Hazard Graph Artificial Intelligence for Infrastructure Resilience Screening in Romania: Integrating Ground Motion, Earth Observation, Hazard Exposure and Network Topology
items.abstract: Natural hazards can disrupt transport infrastructure through spatially heterogeneous flooding, seismic shaking, terrain conditions, and observed ground motion, while local exposure alone does not determine system-wide consequences. This study develops a reproducible multi-hazard Graph Artificial Intelligence framework for infrastructure resilience screening on the Romanian strategic road network. A frozen attributed line graph combines network topology with European land-cover, terrain, seismic, flood, and ground-motion evidence, and an independent disruption simulator provides continuous resilience-loss targets. GCN, GraphSAGE, and GAT were trained under a leakage-controlled three-seed protocol. On the blind 194-scenario PRIMARY TEST, ensemble RMSE/R2 were 0.013343/0.997104 for GCN, 0.013978/0.996822 for GraphSAGE, and 0.015830/0.995924 for GAT. A fresh GCN branch achieved RMSE/R2 = 0.018230/0.995852 on 111 component-disjoint cases and 0.010468/0.991654 on 256 severity-specific held-out cases. On 208 predefined external anchors held out from Graph-AI fitting and selection, GAT attained the lowest ensemble RMSE (0.021620; R2 = 0.975065), while seismic-only transfer remained weak (n = 10; R2 = 0.251–0.386). A frozen six-family GCN ablation (18 checkpoints; 194 matched test scenarios) found RMSE = 0.026175 after seismic feature omission versus 0.013343 for the full-input GCN; this is simulator-specific sensitivity, not causal hazard attribution. The results support accurate emulation of the frozen simulator and transfer-aware screening, not structural safety certification. The model outputs are simulator-based rather than observed disruption outcomes; neither an end-to-end simulator-to-GNN speedup nor calibrated prediction intervals are established by the present evaluation.

items.title: Navigating AI Integration in Final Project Supervision: Academic Integrity, Challenges, and Best Practices
items.abstract: Abstract: This study examines the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the thesis supervision process for students in the Islamic Communication and Broadcasting Study Program at Sulthan Thaha Saifuddin State Islamic University (UIN) Jambi. Employing a qualitative approach, the study involved in-depth interviews with 10 students who were actively completing their undergraduate theses during the 2025/2026 academic year and five thesis supervisors. The findings indicate that the integration of AI provides various benefits, including increased efficiency, more personalized guidance, and improved accessibility to academic references. Students reported that AI accelerated the thesis revision process by providing real-time feedback and recommendations for relevant literature. Meanwhile, lecturers experienced a reduced administrative workload through the automation of routine tasks, allowing them to focus more on providing guidance on conceptual and methodological aspects. The recommendations emphasize the importance of institutional policies to enhance technology training and develop digital infrastructure for academic staff and students. Thus, AI can be effectively integrated to support the thesis supervision process and help students achieve their academic potential more optimally. The main limitation of this study lies in its limited sample size, which prevents the findings from being statistically generalized. items.title: NEP 2020 and Artificial Intelligence: Transforming Teaching, Learning, and Assessment in Higher Education
items.abstract: Abstract India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 articulates an ambitious vision for the comprehensive reform of higher education, foregrounding technology integration, multidisciplinary learning, and learner-centred pedagogy as central pillars. Concurrently, the global proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) across educational domains has prompted serious scholarly and policy-level engagement with its transformative potential and inherent risks. This paper presents a critical analysis of the intersection between NEP 2020 and AI-driven transformation in three core dimensions of higher education: teaching, learning, and assessment. Drawing upon verified policy documents, systematic reviews, and empirical studies published by reputable international bodies and journals between 2016 and 2025, the paper examines how NEP 2020’s policy architecture creates both affordances and constraints for AI adoption. The analysis reveals that while the policy’s emphasis on digital infrastructure, personalised learning, and continuous assessment aligns substantively with global AI-in-education trajectories, significant challenges persist regarding equitable access, faculty preparedness, ethical governance, and assessment integrity. The paper argues that realising NEP 2020’s AI-enabled vision demands a critical, context-sensitive implementation strategy that moves beyond techno-optimism toward principled, evidence-informed integration.

items.abstract: Motorcycle riders face numerous occupational risks as a result of their exposure to road traffic accidents, environmental conditions, and ergonomic difficulties. This study looked at the use of personal protective equipment and occupational hazards by motorcycle riders in Rivers West Senatorial District, Rivers State. Five objectives, five research questions, and two hypotheses were developed and tested to a significance level of 0.05. With a population of 8,595 motorcyclists in Rivers West Senatorial District, Rivers State, and a sample size of 756 motorcyclists from Rivers West's various local governments, the study employed a descriptive cross-sectional survey design. The reliability coefficient of the self-structured questionnaire that was used for data collection was 0.91, and it was validated by three professors in the department of Human Kinetics, Health, and Safety Education. According to the study's findings, the result demonstrated that motorcyclists were particularly susceptible to physical danger (3.06 0.48). The findings of this study are to be expected because riders are exposed to numerous physically hazardous factors while riding. There was a negative correlation because when riders use personal protective devices like nose masks, eye goggles, and protective clothing, they are less likely to be exposed to physical hazards. When riders use PPD, they are more likely to be exposed to more hazards. It was recommended among others that management of road transport workers should put necessary laws to enforce the utilization of personal protective devices like eye goggle, nose masks, reflective and helmet by drivers or riders to reduce exposure to physical hazards and accidents among motorcyclists, the national union of road transport workers NURTW through their various bodies in rural and urban areas should establish regulatory personnel’s to ensure that there is strict compliance to safety by putting on the necessary protective devices by drivers/riders and fine should be paid for those that fail to comply.

items.title: Organisational Best Practices for AI Accountability and Acceptance
items.abstract: The introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into policing comes with some concerns and challenges: concerns from the public, and indeed police leaders, about the nature of its usage in a context of already declining trust and confidence in policing, and amongst staff concerned about changes to working practices and even job security. The implementation of AI into (forces) organisations must therefore come with comprehensive governance and accountability structures and practices to ensure these concerns are considered and addressed, allowing for the effectiveness and efficiency benefits of AI to flourish alongside sustained—or hopefully improving—public trust and confidence levels. This chapter will highlight, discuss and recommend organisational best practices that should be considered by organisations to help them effectively develop or deploy AI systems across a range of operational use cases.

items.title: Practitioner Perceptions of What Is Needed for AI Accountability
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence presents policing with new accountability challenges that extend beyond established legal, organisational and professional standards. This chapter examines expert perceptions of what is needed to make AI accountability meaningful and demonstrable within policing and security contexts. Drawing on primary research with experts from forensics, counter terrorism, serious and organised crime and child sexual exploitation, the chapter identifies accountability as a multi-layered concept involving organisational answerability, process integrity, evidential robustness, professional conduct, legal and ethical justification, auditability, review and challenge. The chapter argues that AI accountability in policing cannot be reduced to compliance with policy or law alone. Instead, it requires a lifecycle-based framework capable of showing how AI systems are governed, evidenced, explained, challenged, corrected and improved. In doing so, the chapter positions expert insight as essential to developing AI accountability arrangements that are usable by police leaders, operational users, procurement teams, oversight bodies, suppliers and affected communities.

items.title: Prevalence of burnout syndrome and associated factors among nurses in Mogadishu, Somalia: a multicenter cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Burnout is a major occupational health concern among nurses, with important implications for workforce well-being, quality of care, and patient safety. However, evidence on its prevalence and associated factors among nurses in Somalia remains limited. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of burnout syndrome and identify associated factors among nurses in Mogadishu, Somalia. Methods A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted between 1 January and 28 February 2026 across five hospitals in Mogadishu. A total of 292 nurses completed an online self-administered questionnaire. Burnout was assessed using the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey (MBI-HSS) and defined as high emotional exhaustion (≥27), high depersonalization (≥13), and low personal accomplishment (≤31). Associations with sociodemographic, occupational, and psychosocial factors were examined using logistic regression. Results are presented as adjusted odds ratios (AORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results A total of 292 nurses participated, of whom 18.2% (95% CI: 13.9–23.1) met the study definition of burnout. In the sociodemographic/occupational model, burnout was associated with mixed shift schedules, longer service duration, chronic illness, and high workload, with the strongest association observed among nurses with >10 years of service (AOR = 3.63, 95% CI: 1.40–9.40). In the psychosocial model, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, poor sleep quality, and job dissatisfaction were associated with burnout, with depressive symptoms showing the strongest association (AOR = 5.85, 95% CI: 2.61–13.14). Conclusion Nearly one in five nurses met the study definition of burnout, with several occupational, psychological, and health-related factors associated with burnout. These findings may inform workplace strategies to support nurses’ well-being, while longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal relationships.

items.title: Professional Identity of Graphic Designers in the Age of Generative AI: Threats, Adaptation, and a Conceptual Typology
items.abstract: Generative AI tools such as Midjourney, Adobe Firefly, and DALL-E are changing how graphic designers work and putting pressure on how they see themselves professionally. Prior research has looked at GenAI’s technical capabilities, its effects on creative industries broadly, copyright questions, and design pedagogy, usually one at a time; few studies connect these threads to ask what GenAI means for graphic designers’ professional identity specifically, and that is the gap this review addresses. The review draws on 33 peer reviewed sources published between 2021 and 2026, from design studies, human computer interaction, organizational psychology, and legal scholarship, located through keyword searches of Consensus, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, and the ACM Digital Library. Sources were grouped around three areas, authorship and creative ownership, skill acquisition, and career prospects, and read against functional identity theory, professional role identity research, and work on human AI collaboration. Out of this comes a typology of three ways designers respond to GenAI: Resisters, Adapters, and Integrators, running from human centered to AI centered practice. GenAI unsettles familiar ideas about authorship, expertise, and creative ownership, and speeds up changes already underway in design workflows. Early career designers appear to face a higher risk of skill loss than experienced ones, who tend to treat GenAI as a complement to their existing competencies rather than a replacement for them. The typology extends functional identity and professional role identity theory into the creative professions, giving other researchers something concrete to test. It should also help in practice: design educators can use it to build GenAI literacy and skill retention into curricula, and designers and professional associations can use it to think through positioning, ethical concerns, and copyright as generative AI becomes part of everyday practice.

items.title: Psychological pathways associated with gamified physical education and perceived learning in adolescents and young adults
items.abstract: Abstract Gamified technology is increasingly used in physical education (PE), but evidence remains fragmented across motivation, engagement, and learning-related outcomes. This study proposed and empirically tested an integrated model linking students’ perceptions of gamified PE with psychological need satisfaction, motivation, multidimensional engagement, and perceived learning outcomes. A cross-sectional survey was completed by 500 secondary and tertiary students (mean age = 18.90 years, SD = 3.77; 51.4% female) from five institutions across three countries. Participants had experienced institution-approved gamified PE platforms sharing points, badges, feedback, challenges, progress indicators, meaningful choice, and cooperative activities, with limited teacher-level variation. A 43-item questionnaire measured 11 reflective constructs; 42 indicators were retained. Data were analyzed using PLS-SEM with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Gamified Technology Use and Perceived Enjoyment were positively associated with autonomy, competence, and relatedness satisfaction. Need satisfaction was positively associated with intrinsic and extrinsic motivation; motivation was positively associated with behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement; and all engagement dimensions were positively associated with perceived learning outcomes. The model explained 58.9% of PLO variance. Direct GTU–PLO and PE–PLO associations were nonsignificant, whereas the specified sequential indirect associations were significant. The findings support a cross-sectional pattern consistent with the proposed framework but do not establish causal or temporal mediation. Mastery-oriented feedback, meaningful task choice, progress tracking, and cooperative missions warrant further experimental evaluation, while public ranking should be used cautiously.

items.title: Quality-aware exploration budget allocation for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning
items.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) requires agents to discover joint strategies in a combinatorially large state-action space, yet effective coordination configurations are exceedingly rare. Intrinsic motivation, which augments task rewards with novelty bonuses, is a popular approach for driving exploration, but its effectiveness hinges on the exploration intensity $β$, where too large a value overwhelms the task signal and causes coordination collapse, while too small a value prevents discovery of rare strategies. We address two complementary challenges: adapting $β$ globally over training, and allocating the exploration budget across agents whose intrinsic reward signals vary in reliability. Our framework combines a return-conditioned sigmoid schedule (RCB) for global intensity control with a per-agent Reward Signal Quality (RSQ) metric that concentrates the exploration budget on agents with reliable signals. The core insight is that agents receiving noisy intrinsic rewards should explore less aggressively, and this allocation can be determined automatically from signal-to-noise statistics. Successor Distance (SD), a quasimetric intrinsic reward, naturally produces distinguishable per-agent signal quality, completing the framework with convergence and ordering preservation guarantees. On seven cooperative benchmarks (MPE, SMAX, MABrax), our method achieves top-tier returns across all environments.

items.abstract: In this chapter, we discuss the gaps in the current understanding of how generative large language models (LLMs) make person judgments. We consider the ethical and legal implications of using LLMs to make person judgments to inform HR decision making. Finally, we outline a set of general research questions centered on unstudied and understudied questions as it pertains to the use of LLMs in HR decision making.

items.title: Real-Time Human-Adaptive Task Allocation for Multi-Human Multi-Robot Supervision
items.abstract: We propose a human-factor-aware method of allocating robot supervision tasks to multiple human operators. In scenarios where multiple operators occasionally teleoperate multiple robots to help the robots overcome difficulties, the allocation of the supervisory control tasks to humans needs to consider the real-time cognitive states of individual operators. However, most existing methods assume fixed supervisory capacity per operator and overlook fluctuations in the human factors such as workload and fatigue. As a result, workload distribution can be unbalanced where some operators become overloaded while the others remain underused. Our method dynamically regulates supervisory capacity and allocates tasks in a way that maintains balanced mental workload, prevents overload, and improves overall team performance. The allocation method uses a greedy strategy that minimizes estimated operator workloads with task prioritization. Robots are assigned to operators by reflecting their current supervisory capacity where the required effort depends on the types of tasks. items.title: Recognising the Benefits and Challenges of AI in Policing
items.abstract: The introduction of AI (Artificial Intelligence) into policing and the wider law enforcement landscape offers real opportunities to improve the service provided to both victims and the wider public. This chapter outlines the core benefits of AI for improving the efficiency, effectiveness and legitimacy of not just policing but the wider criminal justice system. After conducting a detailed analysis of current systems, processes and data sources, the adoption of the correct AI system can support the police in their decision-making to prevent crime, identify and deal with suspects quickly, safeguard vulnerable people, deliver effective services, while also offering potentials for year-on-year cost savings without reducing the quality of provision. However, AI also carries risks and challenges for policing. This chapter argues that establishing clear and transparent internal and external accountability processes is key to underpin the adoption and deployment of AI as part of responsible policing. Competent accountability provisions will support the organisation in gaining the trust, confidence and acceptance of both their own staff and the wider public.

items.title: Reconfiguring graphic design education for generative AI in higher education: a human-agency and adaptive-curriculum framework
items.abstract: Introduction Generative AI creates a curriculum-transformation problem by redistributing activities through which disciplinary expertise is learned, practised, demonstrated, and assessed. This study examines that problem within graphic design education as a bounded empirical case. Methods A survey of 270 participants was analysed using exploratory factor analysis ( N = 265 complete cases), and semi-structured interviews with 12 design academics and practitioners were analysed using a frozen rule-based codebook across 650 meaning units. The quantitative and qualitative strands were analysed independently and integrated through a joint display. Results The quantitative analysis yielded a broad, sample-specific Transformative–Normative response orientation and a narrower Curricular Diagnostic Critique cluster; neither is interpreted as a validated latent construct. The final qualitative dataset contained 504 normative/transformative units (77.5%), 35 diagnostic units (5.4%), and 111 units retained as X0 (17.1%). Both the N-family and D-family occurred in all 12 interviews. Discussion The integrated interpretation informed the Bot-Haus Curriculum Architecture, which organises human creative agency, experiential human–AI practice, adaptive curriculum, critical and ethical governance, foundational design principles, and educational outcomes. The architecture is presented as an empirically informed, theory-guided design proposition developed from the graphic design case, not as a validated causal model. Transfer to other practice-based disciplines remains a proposition for future empirical testing.

items.title: Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real: Guided Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
items.abstract: Building reliable robot capabilities across diverse tasks requires substantial human effort to develop and maintain skills, design rewards, and integrate perception with control. We present Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real (RPG), a framework for autonomous improvement of robot execution systems without updating model weights. RPG identifies manipulation capabilities in an offline dataset and constructs related practice tasks in simulation. During practice, RPG uses execution feedback, privileged simulator state, and available dataset videos to diagnose failures. It develops new reusable symbolic skills, refines existing skills, and revises the system prompt based on these diagnoses. Cross-task evaluation tests individual candidate changes and merged revisions before they are retained for reuse. At test time, a multimodal LLM uses the resulting system prompt and skill library to coordinate perception and robot control. On held-out initializations of 22 manipulation tasks, RPG improves task success from 28.6% after the first practice round to 95.0% after 15 rounds, outperforming all evaluated baselines, including ASPIRE (75.5%) and CaP-Agent0 powered by GPT-6 Astra Pro (60.0%). After a common calibration and hardware-adaptation procedure, the frozen system succeeds in all 30 physical trials, with ten trials on each of three tasks. Project Website: https://rpg-robot.github.io/

items.title: Reputation, Strategy, and Emotion Effects on Generative AI Cooperation: A Comparison Across Reasoning and Non-Reasoning Models
items.abstract: As generative AI (Gen AI) systems take on increasingly autonomous roles in economically and socially consequential interactions, understanding their propensity to cooperate -- and the signals that shape this propensity -- has become essential. We examine cooperative behavior in frontier Gen AI models using the iterated prisoner's dilemma, manipulating counterpart reputation (positive, unknown, negative), strategy (extortion vs. generosity), and non-verbal emotional signaling (facial expressions conveying competitive or cooperative appraisals). In a first study with non-reasoning models (Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o), cooperation was systematically shaped by all three factors, paralleling patterns long documented in human behavioral research, though models varied substantially in how heavily each factor was weighted. A second study with reasoning models (Claude 4.6, Gemini 3, GPT-5.2) revealed a more concentrated reliance on strategy and reputation, a near-elimination of the Potemkin effect observed in non-reasoning models (evidenced by near-uniform cooperation in a diagnostic harmony game), and a more conditional role for emotion consistent with a hierarchical cue-weighting strategy rather than a simple loss of social sensitivity. Reasoning models also showed heterogeneous end-game behavior, ranging from sustained cooperation to systematic last-round defection effect, revealing model-specific exploitability profiles with direct practical relevance for deployment in negotiation and other multi-round interactions. Together, these findings characterize Gen AI models as increasingly sophisticated, though heterogeneous, social actors, and underscore the practical value of developing standardized cooperation benchmarks to inform the responsible deployment of Gen AI in interactive, socially consequential settings.

items.title: Rethinking the Structure of AI Literacy in Generative AI Educational Systems: Descriptive Patterns of Expert Convergence and Heterogeneity
items.abstract: The integration of generative AI into education raises questions about how AI literacy should be organized, particularly as competencies may operate across different functions during human–AI interaction. This study examined the content and structural organization of AI literacy through a focused literature synthesis and a two-round Delphi study with 11 experts. An initial framework comprising three domains—AI Understanding, AI Application, and AI Integration—and nine competencies was developed and iteratively evaluated. Experts generally evaluated the competency content favorably, while their judgments showed greater heterogeneity regarding some aspects of structural representation. In Round 2, experts supported non-exclusive domain relationships (M = 4.45, SD = 0.52) and primary and secondary domain associations (M = 4.73, SD = 0.47), whereas the proposed representation of competency placement and cross-domain applicability showed greater dispersion (M = 3.73, SD = 1.19, IQR = 1.50). This descriptive pattern informed a theoretical interpretation of the three domains as functional rather than mutually exclusive categories. The resulting framework provides a basis for considering how AI literacy competencies may be enacted during human–AI interaction and related to curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, teacher roles, and AI technologies in generative AI-supported educational systems.
